thread.title: Banking Roundup: Wells Fargo finds more homeowners affected by error… BofA sued over Erica… Citi’s new chair

author: I-Chun Chen
title: Banking Roundup: Wells Fargo finds more homeowners affected by error… BofA sued over Erica… Citi’s new chair
text: – Correspondent, Nov 7, 2018, 2:15pm EST The nation’s largest banks — such as JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE: JPM), Bank of America Corp. (NYSE: BAC), Wells Fargo & Co. (NYSE: WFC), Citigroup Inc. (NYSE: C), Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (NYSE: GS) and Morgan Stanley (NYSE: MS) — have operations around the country. Here are recent stories reported by The Business Journals and other media outlets. Wells Fargo uncovers 250 more customers affected by mortgage miscalculations Wells Fargo & Co. says hundreds more customers than previously thought were improperly denied mortgage modifications. About 870 customers were either incorrectly denied a loan modification or were not offered a repayment plan for which they should have qualified between March 15, 2010, and April 30 of this year, Wells Fargo said in a securities filing on Tuesday. The bank attributes the issue to "an automated calculation error.” ( Charlotte Business Journal ) Wells Fargo executives knew auto insurance program was flawed: lawsuit Wells Fargo & Co executives were warned that an auto insurance plan could be overcharging customers four years before the bank scrapped the program, according to a complaint released by a judge this week. Several executives, including then-General Counsel James Strother and chief auditor David Julian, were among the bank officials briefed in 2012 about possible flaws in the auto insurance program that was ended in 2016, according to parts of a class-action lawsuit that were unsealed on Monday. ( Reuters ) Wells Fargo's wealth management head to retire Wells Fargo & Co’s head of wealth management Jay Welker will retire at the end of March after more than two decades with the San Francisco-based bank. Welker joined Wells Fargo in 1988, overseeing regional commercial banking offices for the bank in California. He was named Wells’ wealth management head in 2003, according to a memo seen by Reuters. ( Reuters ) Wells Fargo welcomes Austin startup into clean-energy incubator Austin-based startup Yotta Solar was one of five companies accepted into the fourth cohort of the Wells Fargo Innovation Incubator, which focuses on clean-energy technology, according to an Oct. 31 announcement. With its selection, Yotta Solar will receive up to $250,000 to test its technology in Golden, Colo., at the U.S. Department of Energy National Renewable Energy Laboratory. ( Austin Business Journal ) Wells Fargo Minnesota's CEO Laurie Nordquist on 'dream job' Laurie Nordquist became Wells Fargo Minnesota's new CEO and lead region president for the Upper Midwest in July, replacing longtime Minnesota CEO David Kvamme, who retired. As lead president for the Upper Midwest region, she oversees all community banking operations in eight states. She's also responsible for more than 350 Wells Fargo bank branches and roughly 4,000 employees. ( Minneapolis/St. Paul Business Journal ) Subscriber content Former JP Morgan trader pleads guilty to manipulating US metals markets for years An ex-J.P. Morgan Chase trader has admitted to manipulating the U.S. markets of an array of precious metals for about seven years -- and he has implicated his supervisors at the bank. John Edmonds, 36, pleaded guilty to one count of commodities fraud and one count each of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, price manipulation and spoofing, according to a Tuesday release from the U.S. Department of Justice. Edmonds spent 13 years at New York-based J.P. Morgan until leaving last year, according to his LinkedIn account. ( CNBC ) JPMorgan taps Apple architect for new Park Avenue tower JPMorgan Chase & Co. has picked a lead architect for its new headquarters. Per Bloomberg News, the New York-based banking giant has tapped Foster + Partners — the firm behind Apple Inc.’s (Nasdaq: AAPL) offices — to design its planned Park Avenue tower. Foster + Partners also designed Bloomberg LP’s London headquarters, which opened last year. JPMorgan Chase, touted as the largest U.S. bank by assets, wants to consolidate its global headquarters and build an entirely new 2.5 million-square-foot headquarters at 270 Park Ave. in Midtown, Manhattan. It's expected to reach up to at least 70 stories, or 500 feet (150 meters) taller than the current headquarters. ( New York Business Journal ) JPMorgan's clients can now access Athena trading program J.P. Morgan Chase & Co. is allowing clients access to its Athena trading program to run analytics on their own investments. Teresa Heitsenrether, the bank's global head of custody and fund services, announced that the New York-based bank has sold subscriptions to its Investment Analytics Platform (IAP) to 208 big investors (h/t CNBC).Another 42 clients are expected to sign by year-end. Clients targeted for J.P. Morgan's IAP include pensions, endowments and insurance companies. ( New York Business Journal ) Bank of America faces trademark lawsuit over virtual assistant Erica Charlotte-based Bank of America Corp. is facing a trademark lawsuit over its use of Erica, a virtual financial assistant it rolled out this year. Erica is powered by artificial intelligence and accessible through BofA's mobile app. It helps customers check balance information, manage spending, transfer money and set up in-person appointments. BofA launched Erica in March and completed its rollout to all customers this summer. ( Charlotte Business Journal ) BofA to award bonuses, other incentives to 95% of its employees Bank of America Corp. will give employees making $100,000 or less in annual compensation a one-time cash bonus of $1,000, Chief Executive Brian Moynihan said in a memo obtained by the Charlotte Business Journal . Cash bonuses will be awarded in the first quarter of 2019. Employees making $100,000 to $350,000 in annual compensation will receive between 200 and 500 restricted stock units in the first quarter of 2019. Stocks awards will be determined based on a compensation tier. BofA estimates the incentives will cover about 95% of its roughly 209,000 employees around the globe. ( Charlotte Business Journal ) Citigroup replaces longtime chairman Citigroup Inc. has named former bank regulator John Dugan as chairman. Dugan, 63, will succeed Mike O’Neill on Jan. 1. O’Neill turned 72 last month, making him ineligible for re-election to the board. According to Reuters, Dugan — a former lawyer to the Citigroup board — became director at the company last year. The move to chairman underscores how the New York-based bank keeps the post separate from current chief executive Mike Corbat. The CEOs of Citigroup's big bank rivals — JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Bank of America Corp. — also serve as chairmen of their boards, the report indicated. ( New York Business Journal ) Prosecutors charge former Goldman Sachs bankers in money-laundering case The U.S. Justice Department unsealed charges Thursday stemming from a multibillion-dollar Malaysian sovereign-wealth fund scandal involving two former Goldman Sachs bankers. The indictment was filed in federal court in New York. The investigation centered on 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB), a government-controlled fund that aimed to pursue economic development projects for Malaysia. ( New York Business Journal ) The Fed is relaxing banking rules. What goodies are the banks getting? The Federal Reserve proposed on Wednesday loosening rules for 16 financial institutions, an important move forward in the Trump administration’s effort to roll back bank regulation. The Fed’s proposals would affect banks with $100 billion to $700 billion in assets, including U.S. Bancorp, Capital One and American Express. The changes would not apply to the nation’s eight largest banks, like Bank of America and Goldman Sachs, which have significantly more loans and securities on their balance sheets. ( The New York Times ) Subscriber content NYC-based activist investor builds stake in Deutsche Bank A New York-based activist hedge fund is hoping to stir positive change at Deutsche Bank AG. Hudson Executive Capital LP, led by Douglas Braunstein, reportedly has built about a 3.1 percent stake in Deutsche Bank (NYSE: DB) common shares. This is said to be Hudson’s biggest investment to date, valued at about $620 million. ( New York Business Journal ) U.S. Bancorp used dark-web experts to beat back cyberattack Banks face all sorts of threats from the so-called dark web, the portion of the Internet that's largely anonymous and invisible to most users. But now financial companies are bringing dark-web resources on their side. The Wall Street Journal reports on the growing use of undercover researchers, sometimes posing as cybercriminals, as a way to spot computer network attacks and malware threats ahead of time. The story specifically calls out Minneapolis-based U.S. Bancorp (NYSE: USB) and San Francisco-based Wells Fargo & Co. — though presumably others are using these vendors, too. ( Minneapolis/St. Paul Business Journal ) PNC retail chief says branch banking isn't dead amid technology investments PNC Financial Services Group Inc. employees and customers in Baltimore stand to benefit from the bank's expansion into new cities, head of retail banking Karen Larrimer said. Larrimer was in Baltimore recently to host a town hall with the Pittsburgh-based bank's local employees. The visit marked Larrimer's first trip to Baltimore since becoming PNC's head of retail banking and chief customer officer in 2016. During her meeting with employees, she received multiple questions about PNC's recent launch of its digital business in new markets and move to simplify products and services. ( Baltimore Business Journal ) Subscriber content Fed proposal would lessen regulatory burden on some of Philadelphia's largest banks In an effort to lessen the burden on big commercial lenders that do not have volatile Wall Street businesses, the Federal Reserve last week offered a proposal that will provide relief to several of Philadelphia’s largest banks….The framework establishes distinct categories of standards for large banking organizations, or those with more than $100 billion in total consolidated assets. Those banks with $700 billion or more in assets, essentially the big four U.S. banks JPMorgan Chase & Co., Wells Fargo & Co., Citigroup and Bank of America will not see any change in compliance expectations. ( Philadelphia Business Journal ) Subscriber content Why the CEOs of JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo and U.S. Bank are bullish on Portland Big banks are bullish on Portland. Since August, the CEOs of three of the biggest banks in the country — JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon, Wells Fargo's Tim Sloan and U.S. Bank's Andy Cecere — visited the city to rally employees and meet with customers. Each gave the Business Journal an exclusive interview. ( Portland Business Journal )
